Q: Find strings with longest common prefix A:

I've brought the shortest implementation

def best_prefix_matches(words, query):
    def cpl(w):
        return sum(c1 == c2 for c1, c2 in zip(w, query))

    max_len = max(cpl(w) for w in words)
    return [w for w in words if cpl(w) == max_len and max_len > 0]

Q: Laravel different environment git .env Xampp & Mamp A:

It depends. If you are sharing any resources that hold encrypted data between the two environments, like a database, then you must copy the app_key. This is because Laravel uses the app_key whenever it encrypts something like a user's password or a session ID.

If you don't need to share a database, sessions, etc then you can and should generate a new key for every environment.

You generate a new key by running this command in your site root:

php artisan key:generate

Ideally, you would run this command as the first step in setting up a new environment, before running database seeds or other stuff. This is because if you generate a new key after seeding your database then any password you created in the seeds will be invalid and you'll have to reseed the database.

Q: How to choose an AWS profile when using boto3 to connect to CloudFront A:

TL;DR (a one-liner you want)

client = boto3.Session(profile_name="my-profile").client("cloudfront")

Details

This is a very common AWS/Boto3 confusion. Boto3 does support profiles, but experience tells docs are really bad.

The following patterns worked for me (sorry, no tl;dr)

The core idea

Boto3 does not take a profile name directly in boto3.client().

Instead, Boto3 resolves credentials through a session, and the session is what is bound to a profile.

So the rule is:

Profiles belong to sessions, not clients.

When you do this:

client = boto3.client("cloudfront")

you are implicitly using the default session, which in turn uses:

  • the AWS_PROFILE env var if set, otherwise
  • the default profile in ~/.aws/credentials

Explicit Session with profile

This is the canonical and recommended solution.

import boto3

session = boto3.Session(profile_name="my-profile-name")
client = session.client("cloudfront")

Just this.

Now CloudFront is accessed using my-profile-name.

Works for:

  • CloudFront
  • S3
  • EC2
  • IAM
  • literally every AWS service (as far as I'm concerned; source: voices in my head; but that's not the point)

Verifying which profile is being used

  • If you want to be absolutely sure and perform sanity checks:
credentials = session.get_credentials()
print(credentials.access_key)
  • or:
print(session.profile_name)

Alternative (I [and they] do not recommend for scripts; but, it is useful for CLI parity [Warp!])

It's almost the same, but via environment variables:

export AWS_PROFILE=my-profile-name
python script.py

But this:

  • is global
  • is "first day of school"-type fix
  • makes debugging harder

For library code, notebooks, and reproducibility, the explicit Session(profile_name=...) approach is much better and "cleaner".

Why CloudFront documentation feels... (not) all over?...

CloudFront itself is global, so:

  • no region is required
  • examples are often minimal
  • docs assume default credential resolution

But authentication still follows exactly the same credential chain as every other AWS service.

Nothing special or weird here. Just under-documentation (because they should have hired me).

Q: Simple autoclick script for MacOS A:

In System Events, the click command can't simulate a mouse click at the mouse's current location. AppleScript isn't designed perform an actual act of 'clicking'; instead, AppleScript sends an Apple Event to the system or a process telling it that a click has been performed, so you have to spell out the details of this 'virtual' click, either by specifying specific global screen coordinates, e.g,:

tell application "System Events"
    click at {384, 62}
end tell

or targeting a particular element of a process, e.g.:

tell application "System Events"
    tell process "My Process"
            tell window 1
                    click button 3
            end tell
    end tell
end tell

Making AppleScript perform direct clicks at the current mouse coordinates calls for other tools. You can use AppleScript ObjC to get the current mouse coordinates, or install a third party unix tool (google recommends 'cliclick') and call it from AppleScript's do shell script command.
